Preserve both facts in the candidate: the start/ownership fact (e.g., 'X started/owns their own [business type]') and the specific activity mentioned, so later questions about the person's career history are answerable.

If the memory being updated already covers the activity but not the starting/ownership fact, enrich or update that memory to add the missing explicit start/ownership fact rather than creating a duplicate memory.

Do not infer ownership from vague business mentions alone; only apply when the speaker uses clear self-ownership or founding language such as 'my store', 'my business', 'started my own', or 'opened my'.

payload.name: Vacation location and time extraction
payload.description: When a message contains a vacation photo or travel anecdote that names a city or place together with a relative time phrase such as 'last summer' or 'this summer', retrieve this Skill during extraction.
content: For messages describing a vacation photo or travel experience, extract any explicit location (city, region, or country) mentioned.

Resolve relative time phrases using the message timestamp: 'last summer' means the previous calendar year's summer; if only a city is named, infer the country from common geographic knowledge when confident.

Create or propose an event memory preserving the location, inferred country, approximate season/year, and the fact that it was a vacation; if a matching memory already exists, update it instead of creating a duplicate.
If a message mentions a photo, picture, vacation, trip, or travel and names a place, treat it as evidence that the speaker was at that place during the indicated time.

Resolve relative time expressions (e.g., 'last summer', 'last winter', 'a few years ago') using the message's occurred_at date to compute an absolute time range. Preserve both the resolved time and the original expression when possible.
Extract a memory (event or state) recording the activity (e.g., vacation, travel, visit), the location, and the resolved time range. Include the speaker as the subject.
If only the location is mentioned without a time, still extract a state/event with the place and note the time as unknown rather than skipping the memory.

payload.name: Preserve temporal anchor for in-progress events
payload.description: During extraction of event or state memories, when a message describes an action as currently in progress (e.g., present continuous tense like 'I'm expanding...', 'I'm building...', 'I'm working on...') and no explicit start date is stated, retrieve this Skill to ensure the message timestamp is captured as the event's start date inside the memory content.
content: When the source message uses present-continuous phrasing to describe an ongoing action or effort (e.g., 'I'm expanding my studio's social media presence') and the message carries a timestamp, treat that timestamp as the event's start point and write the date explicitly into the content, e.g., 'as of April 2023' or 'started April 2023'.
Do not rely solely on the world_start metadata field: include the temporal anchor in the content string so that later questions about when the event began can be answered from the memory text alone.
If the message states an explicit date or period (e.g., 'next month', 'last week', 'since 2022'), preserve that phrase or its resolved calendar value in the content as well.

payload.name: Extract emotional anecdote takeaways
payload.description: When a message contains a personal anecdote or story that explicitly states an emotional feeling, bond, or relationship significance (e.g., 'it showed how much I love her'), during extraction from that message, create a candidate memory that captures the emotional takeaway, not just the factual events.
content: When the speaker shares a personal story or memory and includes an explicit evaluative or emotional statement about a person, pet, or object (e.g., 'it really showed how much I love her', 'that meant the world to me'), extract that statement as its own memory candidate, capturing the subject, the emotion/feeling, and the relationship implied.
Do not skip extraction just because the message is narrative or conversational; the emotional takeaway is a valid memory fact (often an event, relationship, or state).

During the CRUD stage, ADD such candidates when they do not already exist in memory; if a related memory already exists, consider MERGE to enrich it with the emotional detail rather than discarding the nuance.

payload.name: Preserve explicit atmosphere, feeling, and activity couplings in events
payload.description: During extraction, when a message describes an event (game, performance, gathering, trip) and contains explicit subjective descriptions of the atmosphere, mood, or the speaker's feelings (e.g., 'electric', 'intense', 'amazing'), or attributes an emotion to a specific activity, retrieve this skill so those descriptors and pairings are preserved in the event memory.
content: When a source message describes an event, identify each distinct claim separately instead of writing one headline-only candidate; subjective descriptions are as durable as objective facts.

If the raw message contains explicit adjectives about the atmosphere, mood, or the speaker's feelings toward the event, include them verbatim or as a close paraphrase in the event candidate's content.

Before finalizing an event candidate, check it against the source message to confirm no explicit claim — objective or subjective — was dropped; if the message states how the atmosphere felt, that must appear in the persisted memory.

Identify explicit attribution clauses where a feeling or evaluation is tied to a specific activity, object, or person (e.g., 'It was <emotion> to <activity>', '<subject> loved <thing>'). Extract the full phrase so the specific referent is preserved; do not replace it with a general summary of the event.

When summarizing an event in a candidate, keep concrete predicates from the source: what the subject found freeing/enjoyable/difficult, what specific activities they did, liked, or felt. If the source pairs an emotion with an activity, record both the activity and the emotion.

At CRUD time, before ADD or UPDATE of an event or preference memory, check that the stored content can answer questions like 'What did <subject> find <emotion>?' or 'What did <subject> like?'. If the specific activity or item is missing, treat the candidate as incomplete and repair it before persisting.

payload.name: Preserve explicit emotional statements and assessments
payload.description: When a message contains explicit emotion words (e.g., relief, excitement, worry, anxiety, hope, fear, joy) or an explicit emotional/evaluative assessment (e.g., 'was a huge success', 'felt great', 'was thrilled', 'loved it') tied to an event, activity, or experience, retrieve this skill during extraction to ensure all stated emotions and their triggers are preserved in memory.
content: Identify explicit emotion vocabulary in the message (relief, excitement, worry, anxiety, hope, fear, joy, anger, etc.) and who experiences it and about what topic.
If the speaker or another person explicitly states their emotions, include the specific emotion terms in the extracted memory content rather than summarizing only the action, plan, or event.
Do not infer emotions beyond what is stated, but do not omit explicitly named emotions; list them as part of the event/state memory (e.g., 'X feels <emotions> about <topic>').

When a message contains both a described event and an explicit emotional or evaluative assessment, create a separate 'state' memory capturing the emotional assessment: subject, the assessment itself preserving the original phrasing, and the context/object it refers to.
Also create the 'event' memory for any factual actions without attempting to merge the assessment into the event content.
If a matching state memory already exists, update it with the new assessment rather than skipping it.

Before marking a candidate as a duplicate or already represented (SKIP), compare the candidate's emotional claims against existing memories. If the candidate contains a stated feeling that no stored memory captures, do not SKIP; instead ADD a new memory or UPDATE/MERGE an existing related memory to include that feeling.

payload.name: Preserve specific evaluative descriptors and attributes
payload.description: When a message expresses a person's opinion or evaluation of an entity, item, or experience and includes specific descriptive qualities or adjectives (e.g., 'rich and creamy', 'super cozy and comfy', 'looks amazing'), retrieve this skill during extraction to preserve those exact descriptors alongside the overall sentiment.
content: Identify direct descriptive or evaluative phrases about the primary entity in the message (e.g., '[entity] looks/feels/seems [adjective]').

When creating or updating a memory of any kind, preserve the specific descriptor(s) verbatim in the content rather than replacing them with a vague paraphrase such as 'expressing excitement' or 'showing support'.

If the entity is a person, place, event, or project mentioned by the speaker, attach the descriptive fact to the relevant memory field (content, attribute, or relationship enrichment) so it is retrievable independently of the broader sentiment.

When extracting an opinion or evaluation, do not collapse the statement into a single generic sentiment word (e.g., 'delicious', 'liked it', 'great'). Identify every distinct evaluative claim the speaker makes.

Preserve the specific descriptive attributes explicitly stated by the speaker (e.g., 'rich and creamy', 'spicy', 'smooth', 'too salty') alongside the overall sentiment, using the speaker's own wording where possible.

Each distinct attribute is a separately queryable claim: write candidate content that keeps them separate, e.g., 'Nate made coconut milk ice cream, found it super good, and described it as rich and creamy.' rather than merging them into 'found it delicious'.

payload.name: Preserve explicit media evaluations
payload.description: When a message names a specific movie, game, show, or book AND includes a strong explicit evaluation (e.g., 'blew my mind', 'loved it'), retrieve to preserve the exact evaluative claim. Limited to messages with both a named entertainment item and an emotive verdict; do not trigger on neutral mentions.
content: When a message names a specific entertainment item (movie, game, show, book) and includes an explicit strong evaluation, extract BOTH the factual claim (item was seen/played/read) AND the evaluation as separate, verbatim-preserved facts; do not collapse the evaluation into a generic phrase like 'enjoyed for its immersive experience'.
Keep the user's own intensity words (e.g., 'blew my mind', 'loved', 'hated') in the memory content rather than softening or paraphrasing them, since future questions may target the exact sentiment.

If the message contains multiple distinct claims about the same item (e.g., watched it AND it blew his mind), include every distinct claim in the extracted candidate content, not just the first or most neutral one.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-disclosed preferences and favorites
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit first-person statement of liking, loving, enjoying, or a favorite (e.g., 'I love', 'my favorite is', 'I enjoy'), retrieve during extraction to create a preference memory for each distinct item named, preserving modifiers and relational context.
content: Scan every processed message for explicit preference statements using signals such as 'favorite', 'love', 'like', 'prefer', 'enjoy', 'best', or 'go-to' followed by an item, activity, or person.

When such a statement is found, always generate a preference memory candidate capturing: the speaker, the preferred item, the preference strength (e.g., favorite/like/love), and the statement's timestamp.

For each distinct item named in a preference statement, create a separate preference candidate. Preserve the item name exactly as stated, including all qualifiers and modifiers (e.g., 'dairy-free chocolate mousse', not just 'mousse').
If the statement positions the item relative to another favorite (e.g., 'besides coconut milk ice cream'), record that relational context as a qualifier or note on the preference memory.
If the same turn contains both a preference statement and an action (e.g., recommending), emit both a preference memory and an event memory; do not let the event subsume the preference.
Do not skip extraction because another favorite was already mentioned or because the preference is embedded in a longer turn about unrelated topics.

payload.name: Preserve actor and reason in interpersonal events
payload.description: Use during extraction from a message that reports an interpersonal event (e.g., someone mocked, teased, criticized, praised, or helped someone). Retrieve when the memory candidate describes such an action but may omit who performed it or the specific attribute/reason stated.
content: When a message explicitly names people who performed an action toward the speaker or another person (e.g., 'my friends mocked my weight'), include those people and the exact stated reason/topic in the event candidate content, not just a general summary like 'being mocked about his weight'.
Preserve precise descriptive terms from the message (e.g., 'overweight' rather than 'weight') and relative time anchors (e.g., 'last Friday') so the event remains answerable later.
Do not add unrelated details; preserve only the actor(s), the action, the reason/topic, and the time reference explicitly present in the message.

payload.name: Preserve_All_Explicit_Goals
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message enumerates multiple distinct goals, plans, or aspirations from the same speaker, especially with words like 'also', 'and', or 'I want to'. Also applies when updating an existing goal/plan memory and the new message introduces an additional goal alongside a known one.
content: When a message contains multiple explicit goals, plans, or aspirations, extract each distinct item separately rather than merging them into one broader or related concept.
Preserve the speaker's own phrasing for each goal, even if one goal overlaps with an existing memory; do not omit an explicit goal in favor of related advice, interpretation, or alignment details.
If enriching an existing memory, append the newly stated distinct goal to the content instead of replacing the prior goal focus with only the related commentary.
When uncertain whether two stated items are the same goal, prefer separate candidates so no explicitly named goal is lost.

payload.name: Preserve all event participants from plural subject references
payload.description: Use during extraction of event memories when a message describes an activity with a first-person plural subject (we, us, our), or names more than one person as doing something together. Ensures the extracted event records every participant, not just the primary speaker or a single known person.
content: When extracting an event, resolve pronouns and subject phrases to all individuals they refer to. If the speaker says 'we', 'us', or 'our' for a shared activity, include the speaker and the partner/companion(s) as participants in the memory content unless evidence clearly limits the action to the speaker alone.

If the message context establishes a specific co-participant (e.g., a partner, friend, family member) and an activity is described with a plural subject, name both participants explicitly in the extracted event content rather than writing the event as if only one person took part.

For event memories, preserve participant scope in the content string (e.g., list all people involved) and set the subject to the primary speaker when the memory kind requires a single subject, but do not omit co-participants from the recorded event.

payload.name: Preserve explicitly attributed value statements
payload.description: When a session message contains an explicit statement that a specific person (e.g., a family member, mentor, friend) stressed, taught, or emphasized a value or principle, and especially when the speaker says they want to keep it in mind for their work or projects, retrieve this Skill during extraction to ensure the specific attributed claim is captured as its own memory.
content: If a message contains a direct attribution such as '[person] stressed/taught/emphasized the value of X', extract a memory entry whose subject is the speaker and whose content names both the person who expressed the value and the specific value or principle (e.g., helping others, hard work, honesty).

Do not merge such a claim into a general summary of the whole conversation (e.g., 'they discussed the influence of loved ones') — the attributed value is the durable, queryable fact and must appear verbatim enough to answer 'What did [person] stress the value of?'.
If the speaker connects the value to an application (e.g., 'keep in mind for my engineering projects', 'want to use in my work'), include that stated application in the same memory entry.
Only create this focused entry when the attribution is explicit in the message; do not infer values that were merely implied.

payload.name: Preserve co-participants in shared events
payload.description: During extraction of event memories, when a message describes a trip, retreat, or activity in which the speaker participated together with another person (phrases like 'my partner and I', 'we went', 'with [name]'), retrieve this skill to ensure the named companion is preserved in the extracted memory.
content: When a message explicitly indicates the speaker did something together with another person (e.g., 'my partner and I traveled...', 'we attended...', '... with [name]'), the extracted event memory must include that companion as a co-participant; do not summarize the event as the speaker's solo activity.

Preserve the companion's identity and role as stated (partner, spouse, friend, family member, etc.) and phrase the event content as a joint activity, e.g., '<Subject> and <companion> traveled to <destination> for <duration>', so the memory answers queries about either participant or the pair together.

When the message is the first evidence of a durable relationship (e.g., the speaker has a partner), reflect that relationship within the event content rather than omitting it; only create a separate relationship memory if the relationship fact is clearly durable and not already captured.

payload.name: Preserve concrete details of reported interactions
payload.description: When a message reports a direct interaction with another person (skyped, met, talked, called, hung out, etc.) and names specific topics, content, or items that were shared or discussed, this Skill applies during extraction. It targets messages where the interaction is described with concrete detail, not merely a general statement of friendship or shared hobbies.
content: When a speaker reports a concrete interaction with another person (e.g., skyped, met, talked, called), extract an event memory that records: who participated, the medium of interaction (Skype, phone, in person, etc.), and the specific topics or content discussed or shared (e.g., particular characters, books, projects, items). Do not let a generic relationship memory about friendship or broad shared interests replace these concrete event details.

If the same message also supports a relationship fact (e.g., friendship, reconnecting), add or enrich that relationship memory as appropriate, but always include the specific interaction details in a separate event candidate so the shared content remains queryable.

When in doubt about whether a detail is durable, prefer preserving the specific shared topic/content over summarizing it away into a vague interest; a concrete event fact is more likely to answer future questions than an abstract relationship statement.

payload.name: Preserve_Concrete_Object_Facts
payload.description: Use during extraction when a user message describes an activity or routine and also mentions a concrete object, accessory, clothing, or item associated with a person, pet, or event (e.g., dressing a pet in something, using gear during an activity). Also applies when a single message contains multiple distinct claims about the same subject and a drafted candidate covers only one of them.
content: Extract every distinct factual claim in a source message; do not let the most salient topic (e.g., hiking, playdates) cause you to omit concrete details such as objects, accessories, or items associated with the subject.

If the message mentions clothing, accessories, or equipment worn by or used with a pet or person (e.g., an item put on 'for fun'), capture that fact explicitly inside a candidate's content or as its own separate candidate.

Before finalizing a candidate, reread the source message and verify that no concrete noun fact (an object the subject uses, wears, or interacts with) is left out; if the drafted candidate omits such a fact, amend its content or add an additional candidate.

payload.name: PreserveDirectQuotesForEvents
payload.description: During extraction, when a message contains a speaker's direct quotation that expresses feeling, commitment, or an intention tied to an upcoming event, retrieve this Skill to guide memory content creation.
content: When extracting an event or relationship memory from a message containing a direct quote, preserve the exact quoted wording inside the memory content rather than replacing it with a paraphrase.
Include the speaker and the event context around the quote (e.g., 'Gina said to Jon: "..." about the grand opening') so the memory records both the fact and the verbatim statement.
If the quote is emotionally significant or likely to be asked verbatim later, favor retaining the quote even when the memory is later enriched or updated.

payload.name: Preserve disclosure recipients in direct-address messages
payload.description: During extraction, when a message explicitly addresses a named person (by name, greeting, or direct 'I told you...' / 'guess what') and reveals a personal event or state change, also capture the relationship fact that the speaker informed that addressee about the event.
content: When a message contains a direct address to a named individual (e.g., 'Hey Sam!', 'Sam, guess what?') followed by a disclosure of a personal event or state (marriage, birth, move, job change, illness, etc.), extract not only the event/state memory but also an explicit relationship or state memory recording that the speaker told that named person about it (subject: speaker, object: addressee, relation: 'told/informed about <event>').

For each disclosed event in a direct-address message, check whether the message implies the addressee was previously unaware and is now being informed; if so, preserve the act of telling as part of the candidate content (e.g., 'Evan told Sam that he got married').

If multiple recipients are mentioned across a conversation (e.g., work friends, family), extract each inform-recipient separately with its own evidence source rather than merging them into a generic 'people were told' statement.

payload.name: Preserve entity reactions to conditions
payload.description: When a message states how a person, pet, or other entity reacts to a condition, event, or environment (e.g., dogs hate snow, was confused, loves rain), during extraction keep that specific reaction as its own memory content rather than folding it into a general ownership or preference statement.
content: When extracting from a message, identify explicit statements about how an owned or related entity (pet, family member, etc.) behaves or feels toward a specific condition, event, or object. Preserve the reaction as a distinct fact (e.g., 'Audrey's dogs react to snow with confusion') even if the message also contains ownership details or general preferences.

Do not let a broader preference summary (e.g., 'She prefers sunny days over snowy conditions') replace the entity-specific reaction. Include both the subject and the target condition in the extracted content so the fact can answer later questions about that entity's behavior.

In the extraction candidate, separate facts: one memory for ownership/identity, another for the entity's reaction/behavior toward the specific condition. If the reaction is short-lived or event-bound, prefer an event or state memory; if it is a stable trait, use a profile memory.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated professional activities
payload.description: Retrieve during extraction when a message describes a person's professional development or experience and lists more than one distinct activity (e.g., presenting at a conference, attending workshops, studying, networking, interning). Trigger on observable enumerations of activities in a single message, not on single-activity statements.
content: When a message explicitly lists multiple professional activities or experiences performed by the same person, extract each distinct activity as its own memory candidate (or include all enumerated activities in the candidate content); do not collapse the list into a single headline event.
For each enumerated activity, create a separate event memory with the person as subject, the activity as content, and world_start set to the message's timestamp when no other date is given.

Before finalizing a candidate for a message that names several activities, re-read the message and verify that every explicitly named activity appears in the candidate set; a missing activity is an extraction failure even if the headline activity was captured.

payload.name: PreserveExactEvaluativeDescriptors
payload.description: During extraction of event or relationship memories, when a message contains a person's direct evaluative description of an experience, team, bond, or relationship using a specific adjective or phrase, retrieve this Skill to keep that exact wording in the stored content.
content: When extracting an event or relationship memory, check whether the speaker explicitly evaluates something with a vivid adjective or phrase (e.g., describing an experience, team, or bond). If so, preserve that descriptor verbatim in the candidate content; do not replace it with a paraphrase, general summary, or weaker synonym.

During later UPDATE or enrichment decisions, retain the original evaluative descriptor unless a newer message directly contradicts or explicitly changes it. While rewording other event details, do not silently drop the stored exact wording.

payload.name: Preserve explicit conversation topics before duplicate skip
payload.description: When a message explicitly names the topics, subjects, or items of a conversation, activity, or memory (e.g., 'we chatted about dreams and life'), during extraction of event/state memories; and during CRUD decisions whenever a candidate is about to be SKIPped as duplicate. Narrow scope: only for messages that enumerate specific named details that a paraphrase could lose.
content: During extraction, when the source message explicitly enumerates topics or subjects of a conversation or activity, preserve each named item verbatim in the candidate content (e.g., record 'dreams and life' as stated). Do not replace enumerations with a generic paraphrase such as 'reflecting on life' or 'life topics'.

During CRUD, before SKIPping a candidate as duplicate or already represented, check that an existing memory actually contains every specific detail present in the candidate/raw evidence. If any named detail is missing, do not SKIP: MERGE the candidate's specific details into the closest existing memory, or ADD the candidate as a new memory.

payload.name: Preserve follow-up events with referred-back contacts
payload.description: Retrieve during extraction when a message refers back to a previously mentioned person or entity with a definite reference (e.g., 'that Harry Potter fan I met in CA') and describes a reconnection or new interaction; also when a message is dominated by one relationship/event and may contain other distinct facts about different people or entities.
content: When a message refers to someone with a known reference ('that ... I met', 'the ... from earlier'), create an event candidate recording the re-engagement with that specific person, not just a relationship with the current addressee.

If the earlier interaction already exists in memory, prefer an UPDATE/enrichment that includes the reconnection fact and the computed time interval between the two events (e.g., 'reconnected about three weeks later') when both dates are known.
When a message is dominated by one relationship, still extract other distinct facts in the same message as separate candidates—do not drop secondary events about other referred-to people or entities.

payload.name: Preserve explicit help requests
payload.description: Use when a message contains a direct request or question asking a named or implied person for help, assistance, or support on a specific topic. Trigger during extraction of event memories from such messages.
content: When a message contains an explicit request or question asking someone for help (e.g., 'Can we talk about X?', 'Will you help me with Y?'), extract an event memory that records: who asked, who was asked, the exact topic/task requested, and the date/time if present.
Do not collapse the request into only a general need or struggle (e.g., 'expressing a need for help'); include the direct ask and the specific topic named in the message.

If a second candidate already captures related context (e.g., reaching out to a supporter), keep the explicit request as a separate event candidate unless it is fully redundant with an existing memory.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitImportanceBeliefs
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement from a participant that something is the key, essential, or critical to reaching a goal or desired outcome (e.g., 'X is the key to Y'), use this skill during extraction so the belief is captured as a preference memory.
content: During extraction, when a speaker states that a particular action, trait, or experience is the key/essential/critical factor for achieving a goal or outcome (pattern: '<factor> is the key to <outcome>'), create a candidate memory.
Record the speaker as the subject, the factor as the belief/importance item, and preserve the linked outcome or reason in the memory content.
Do not restrict this rule to statements about the user; capture such beliefs from any participant in the conversation.
If a memory for the speaker already exists, create an UPDATE candidate that adds or refreshes this stated belief rather than skipping it.

payload.name: Preserve direct-address nicknames
payload.description: When a message contains one speaker directly addressing another by a name or shortened nickname (e.g., 'Hey Jo, ...'), during extraction of that message, ensure the nickname/address form is captured as a relationship memory rather than being omitted in favor of only the message's main event.
content: During extraction, treat a vocative name (the term used to call or greet the other person) as extractable signal: if it is a personal name or a shortened form of a participant's name, create or update a relationship memory recording that the speaker uses this nickname for the addressee.

Do not drop the nickname just because the message also contains a more salient event, state, or plan; preserve both by including the nickname fact in the same candidate or as a separate relationship candidate.
Only extract nicknames actually used in direct address and clearly referring to a known participant; ignore generic greetings or titles unless they function as a recurring personal name form.

payload.name: PreserveObjectContentDescriptions
payload.description: During extraction, when a message contains a demonstrative/definite reference to an object (map, photo, document, item, artifact) followed by a description of its subject matter or content (e.g., 'It's a map of X', 'This is a photo of Y'), create a candidate that captures the object and its description.
content: When a speaker uses 'it', 'this', 'that', or a definite noun phrase to refer to an object already mentioned or shown in the conversation, and then states what that object depicts, contains, or represents, extract a candidate.
The candidate should preserve the specific content fact, e.g., for 'It's a map of Middle-earth from LOTR', record that the map is of Middle-earth from LOTR, not merely that a map exists.
If the object was introduced in an earlier turn (e.g., 'Tim shows John a map'), do not skip the later description; the object's content is a distinct, memory-worthy fact.
When the speaker describing the object is also the owner or holder (from context), include a relationship or state linking the speaker to the object, if evidence supports it.

payload.name: PreservePhotoSharingInEvents
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from a message that contains deictic cues indicating the speaker is sharing a photo or image (such as 'Here are', 'Here is a picture of', 'Check out this photo', 'See attached', 'Look at this picture'), retrieve this Skill to ensure the photo-sharing act and its subject are preserved.
content: If the message uses deictic media-sharing wording (e.g., 'Here are', 'Here's a photo of', 'Check out this', 'See attached', 'Look at this picture') that signals the speaker is sharing a visual, include in the extracted event memory both the action of sharing the photo/image and the subject depicted. For example, record 'Nate shared a photo of colorful bowls of coconut milk ice cream' rather than only 'Nate made colorful bowls of coconut milk ice cream'.

When the phrase 'Here is/Here are' appears but no explicit word like 'photo' or 'picture' is used, still treat it as a photo-sharing cue if the surrounding context indicates the speaker is presenting a visual (e.g., the content is a concrete object being shown). Only skip this if the message is clearly a purely verbal description with no evidence of visual sharing.

payload.name: Preserve specific qualifiers and enumerated details in recommendations
payload.description: When a message contains a recommendation, preference, or advice that includes concrete attributes, qualifiers, or enumerated items (e.g., 'fluffy', 'open-world', 'acrylic paints, brushes'), retrieve during extraction to ensure each specific detail is preserved in the memory content.
content: When extracting a recommendation, preference, or advice, list every attribute or qualifier the speaker explicitly assigned to an item (e.g., 'can sit multiple people', 'fluffy', 'a little bit of weight to it') instead of summarizing with a vague umbrella term.

Preserve the speaker's concrete qualifiers in faithful wording: if the source says 'a blanket that has a little bit of weight to it', record it as 'weighted blanket' or equivalently specific phrasing.

If a message contains a recommendation or offer that names specific items (e.g., 'get acrylic paints, brushes, a canvas/paper, and a palette'), include every named item in the candidate content; do not replace the list with a generic phrase.
When multiple items are mentioned, keep each item's descriptor with that item rather than collapsing them into a generic list.

Before committing an UPDATE or MERGE, compare the proposed content against the source message for enumerated attributes; if any stated qualifier is absent, add it so future queries about that attribute can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve shared picture attribution
payload.description: When a message describes a picture, image, or visual that the user shared or is sharing, and also identifies its creator, artist, or source, use this during extraction of the message.
content: If a message contains an explicit sharing/display action (e.g., 'shared', 'that picture is', 'here's a photo') plus a source/creator attribution, extract an event memory that preserves the subject, the act of sharing, the picture, and the creator/source attribution.
Do not reduce the fact to only 'owns/describes an item by X'; keep the sharing event and attribution as a distinct part of the memory content.
When the message states that the creator made or produced the pictured object (e.g., 'they created all the props'), include that production attribution in the memory.

During CRUD enrichment, if an existing memory already contains the same object/creator but lacks the sharing event, update it to add the sharing fact rather than treating the existing memory as sufficient.

payload.name: Preserve explicit skill-acquisition facts
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement of how someone acquired a skill or ability (e.g., 'I taught myself', 'I learned on my own', 'my mom taught me'), during extraction ensure that acquisition fact is preserved in the memory candidate, not just the accompanying context like passion, support, or encouragement.
content: Identify explicit statements about how a skill or ability was acquired, especially self-directed learning phrases (e.g., 'I taught myself', 'learned on my own', 'self-taught').

When a message mixes such an acquisition fact with contextual details (e.g., age, parental support, enthusiasm), the extracted candidate must include the acquisition fact itself, naming the skill and the mode of acquisition (e.g., 'Jolene taught herself to play the console') rather than replacing it with a general summary.
If the message conveys multiple distinct durable facts (acquisition plus supporting context), either keep them together in one candidate or create separate candidates so no explicit fact is dropped.
Before finalizing an event or preference candidate, check that no explicit claims in the source message were omitted in favor of background detail.

payload.name: Preserve subject role in shared activities
payload.description: During extraction or update of event memories, when a message describes a shared or social activity (e.g., playdate, outing, group walk, meetup, class) and the user explicitly states their own action alongside someone else's action in the same sentence or clause.
content: When extracting an event about a shared or social activity, capture the subject's own stated role or activity (e.g., chatting with people, relaxing, exercising) in addition to the setting and other participants' actions; do not let companions' actions (e.g., dogs making new friends) replace the subject's action.

Before finalizing a candidate, re-scan the source message for clauses describing what the subject personally does during the activity (often introduced by 'for me to...', 'I get to...', 'it lets me...') and include that detail.

When UPDATE or MERGE enriches an existing event memory from a message about a shared activity, verify the new content still contains the subject's own stated action; if missing, add it rather than carrying forward only the companions' actions.

payload.name: Verify evidence before SKIP in CRUD decisions
payload.description: Retrieve during the CRUD decision stage when a candidate is about to be SKIPped with a redundancy-based reason such as 'already included', 'already covered', 'duplicate', or 'already fully represented'. Use when deciding whether to discard an extracted fact without persisting it.
content: Before choosing SKIP for a candidate with a redundancy justification, verify that a concrete existing memory version actually contains the same fact (subject, predicate/object, and relevant time bounds). Check the current memory snapshot and committed change events; a candidate pending in the same batch does not count as existing.
If no covering memory exists, do not SKIP: ADD the candidate as a new memory, or MERGE/UPDATE into a partially covering memory to preserve the new fact.

If the candidate contains any fact not explicitly present in stored content (e.g., an emotional state, attribute, or distinct project), do not skip the whole candidate; preserve the uncovered fact via UPDATE or ADD.
Treat 'overlap' as meaning the same specific fact, artifact, event, or project. Sharing a broad domain (e.g., both are 'writing') is not overlap; a distinct item must be persisted.

When issuing a duplicate SKIP, always identify the target_memory_id of the memory that already represents the candidate's content. A SKIP with no verifiable existing memory is an error and must be replaced with an ADD.
Evaluate each candidate independently within a batch: confirming one candidate as covered does not imply that other candidates from the same message are covered.
